```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

# Synthetic teaching data for BIOS 6301. Not real patients.
set.seed(6301)
n <- 60
trial <- data.frame(
  id        = sprintf("P%03d", 1:n),
  arm       = rep(c("Placebo", "Treatment"), each = n / 2),
  site      = sample(1:4, n, replace = TRUE),
  age       = round(rnorm(n, 61, 9)),
  sex       = sample(c("F", "M"), n, replace = TRUE),
  weight_kg = round(rnorm(n, 82, 15), 1),
  sbp_0     = round(rnorm(n, 148, 14)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
trial$sbp_12 <- round(trial$sbp_0 -
  ifelse(trial$arm == "Treatment", rnorm(n, 14, 8), rnorm(n, 3, 8)))

# Repeated-measures version of the same cohort, for the resampling-unit demo:
# three visits per patient, a large patient-level random intercept (SD 12) and
# small within-patient noise (SD 4). Nothing is "broken" here — the data are
# simply clustered, which is what makes the row bootstrap wrong.
set.seed(2024)
patient_effect <- rnorm(n, 0, 12)
trial_long <- data.frame(
  id   = rep(trial$id, each = 3),
  arm  = rep(trial$arm, each = 3),
  week = rep(c(4, 8, 12), times = n),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
trial_long$sbp <- round(140 + rep(patient_effect, each = 3) +
  ifelse(trial_long$arm == "Treatment", -10, 0) + rnorm(n * 3, 0, 4))

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 15))
gold <- "#CFAE70"
```

## The statistical computing sequence {.smaller}

| Session | Question | Main product |
|---|---|---|
| 14 · Simulation | How does a method behave when the truth is known? | A checked simulation study |
| 15 · Resampling | What can repeated use of observed data tell us? | Uncertainty and held-out performance |
| 16 · Practical analysis | How do we fit, inspect, and deliver an analysis? | Models, numerical checks, and an auditable handoff |

Functions, validation, and iteration from Sessions 11–13 support all three.

## Learning goals {.smaller}

- Match bootstrap, permutation, and cross-validation to their targets.
- Compute bootstrap SE, bias, and intervals; assess stability and limitations.
- State an exchangeability or randomization argument before permuting.
- Preserve participants, pairs, or clusters in resampling and validation.
- Generate held-out predictions with preprocessing fitted inside each training fold.
- Separate model selection from final performance evaluation.

## Session outline {.smaller}

| Block | Content |
|---|---|
| 1 | Three resampling targets |
| 2 | Bootstrap estimates and intervals |
| 3 | Bootstrap limitations and stability |
| 4 | Permutation tests and exchangeability |
| 5 | Participants, clusters, and pairs |
| 6 | Cross-validation and preprocessing |
| 7 | Model comparison, validation design, and lab |

# 1 · Resampling targets {.section-divider}

## Three resampling targets {.smaller}

| Method | Repeated operation | Target |
|---|---|---|
| Bootstrap | Sample observational units with replacement | Sampling uncertainty of an estimate |
| Permutation | Reassign labels under a valid null scheme | Null reference distribution of a statistic |
| Cross-validation | Fit on training data; predict held-out data | Performance on new observations |

Replacement alone does not determine validity. Specify the target, the unit,
and which relationships the repeated operation must preserve.

## The same line of code, twice {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: two-samples
sbp <- c(150, 142, 168, 131, 155)

set.seed(1)
sample(sbp, replace = TRUE)   # bootstrap: some values twice, some not at all
sample(sbp)                   # permutation: same values, new order
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
- **With replacement:** values may repeat or be omitted.
- **Without replacement:** same values, new order. This changes their pairing
  with labels, arms, or times.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
For `length(x) > 1`, `sample(x)` permutes the values.
To sample positions in code, prefer `sample.int(length(x))`.
:::


# 2 · The bootstrap, by hand {.section-divider}

## Why it works at all {.smaller}

The thing you want is a property of the **population**: the standard deviation of
your estimator across repeated samples from it.

. . .

You do not have the population. You have one sample — which is your best available
estimate of it.

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**The plug-in principle.** Wherever the formula says *population*, substitute the
*empirical distribution of your sample*, and compute.
:::

. . .

::: {.smaller}
So: resample from your data exactly as nature sampled from the population — same
size *n*, drawn with replacement — and watch how the statistic moves.
:::


## Resample, recompute, collect {.smaller}

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-width: 10
flowchart LR
  D["<b>your data</b><br/>n = 60"] --> R["<b>resample</b><br/>n = 60,<br/>with replacement"]
  R --> S["<b>recompute</b><br/>the statistic"]
  S --> C["<b>collect</b><br/>one number"]
  C -.->|"B = 2000 times"| R
  C --> H["<b>bootstrap<br/>distribution</b>"]
  style D fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#CFAE70
  style R fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff
  style S fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
Three lines of code, and none of them are new. `sample()` is Session 14, indexing
a data frame by a vector of row numbers is Session 4, and `replicate()` is a
functional from Session 13.
:::


## The statistic, as a function {.smaller}

We want the **difference in median** 12-week SBP between arms. There is no
convenient formula for its standard error — which is exactly when the bootstrap
earns its keep.

```{r}
#| label: med-diff
# Difference in median sbp_12, Treatment minus Placebo.
# Takes a data frame with `arm` and `sbp_12`; returns one number.
med_diff <- function(data) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(data), all(c("arm", "sbp_12") %in% names(data)))
  median(data$sbp_12[data$arm == "Treatment"]) -
    median(data$sbp_12[data$arm == "Placebo"])
}

obs_med <- med_diff(trial)
obs_med
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
Statistic first, resampling second. If the function is wrong, 2000 resamples make
it wrong 2000 times.
:::


## Bootstrap within treatment arms {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: boot-med
set.seed(14)
B <- 2000

boot_med <- replicate(B, {
  groups <- split(seq_len(nrow(trial)), trial$arm)
  idx <- unlist(lapply(groups, function(i)
    i[sample.int(length(i), length(i), replace = TRUE)]))
  med_diff(trial[idx, ])
})

str(boot_med)
head(round(boot_med, 1))
```

## The same within-arm bootstrap with dplyr {.smaller}

::: {.smaller}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="The tidyverse way — same thing"}
```r
purrr::map_dbl(seq_len(B), \(i) med_diff(
  trial |> dplyr::group_by(arm) |>
    dplyr::slice_sample(prop = 1, replace = TRUE) |> dplyr::ungroup()))
```
:::
:::


## What came back {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: fig-boot-med
#| fig-cap: "Bootstrap distribution of the difference in median SBP at 12 weeks."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| echo: false
ggplot(data.frame(stat = boot_med), aes(stat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = gold, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs_med, linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = obs_med, y = Inf, label = "  observed", hjust = 0,
           vjust = 1.6, size = 4.5) +
  labs(x = "Difference in median SBP (mmHg)", y = "Resamples")
```

::: {.smaller}
Centred near the observed value. Ragged, because a median of 30 integers can only
land on so many values.
:::


## The bootstrap standard error {.smaller}

The standard deviation of the resampled statistics **is** the estimated standard
error. That is the whole definition.

```{r}
#| label: boot-se
se_boot <- sd(boot_med)
se_boot
```

. . .

```{r}
#| label: boot-bias
mean(boot_med) - obs_med    # bootstrap estimate of bias
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
This is bias relative to the empirical distribution of the observed sample. It is not the true bias measured against a known population parameter in Session 14.
:::


## Percentile and basic intervals {.smaller}

```{r}
perc <- quantile(boot_med, c(.025, .975))
basic <- 2 * obs_med - quantile(boot_med, c(.975, .025))
rbind(percentile = unname(perc), basic = unname(basic))
```

- **Percentile:** use quantiles of the bootstrap estimates directly.
- **Basic:** reflect those quantiles around the observed estimate.
- Both rely on a suitable bootstrap approximation; neither automatically has
  95% coverage in small, biased, or irregular problems.

Compare endpoints and assumptions. Do not choose whichever interval gives a preferred conclusion.

## Check it where you know the answer {.smaller}

The bootstrap is most trustworthy when you have first watched it reproduce a
result you can verify.

```{r}
#| label: boot-vs-t
mean_diff <- function(data) {
  mean(data$sbp_12[data$arm == "Treatment"]) -
    mean(data$sbp_12[data$arm == "Placebo"])
}

```

## Compare the bootstrap and Welch standard errors {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: boot-vs-t-compare
set.seed(17)
boot_mean <- replicate(B, {
  groups <- split(seq_len(nrow(trial)), trial$arm)
  i <- unlist(lapply(groups, function(j) j[sample.int(length(j), replace = TRUE)]))
  mean_diff(trial[i, ])
})

c(boot_se = sd(boot_mean),
  welch_se = t.test(sbp_12 ~ arm, data = trial)$stderr)
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
Agreement for the mean is a useful code check. It does not establish that a bootstrap interval for a different statistic has correct coverage.
:::


## Bootstrap stability {.smaller}

More resamples reduce computational variation; they do not add participants
or repair an inappropriate bootstrap scheme.

```{r}
boot_interval <- function(seed, B = 1000) {
  set.seed(seed)
  groups <- split(seq_len(nrow(trial)), trial$arm)
  ans <- replicate(B, {
    i <- unlist(lapply(groups, function(j)
      j[sample.int(length(j), replace = TRUE)]))
    med_diff(trial[i, ])
  })
  unname(quantile(ans, c(.025, .975)))
}
```

## Compare interval endpoints across seeds {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: bootstrap-stability-runs
t(vapply(1501:1503, boot_interval, numeric(2)))
```

Check endpoints across documented seeds and larger `B`; keep all runs, not the best-looking one.

# 3 · When the bootstrap fails {.section-divider}

## Limits of the ordinary bootstrap {.smaller}

| Situation | Why extra resamples do not solve it |
|---|---|
| Very small samples | The empirical distribution may poorly represent the population |
| Extremes or boundary parameters | The ordinary bootstrap approximation can fail |
| Heavy tails | Usual finite-variance approximations may fail even though a sampling distribution exists |
| Dependent rows | Independent row resampling destroys the study's dependence |

A smooth histogram is not proof of validity. Simulation in a relevant known-truth
setting can evaluate coverage; the sampling design determines the resampling unit.

## The maximum, bootstrapped {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: boot-max
set.seed(18)
boot_max <- replicate(B, max(trial$sbp_0[sample(nrow(trial), replace = TRUE)]))

length(unique(boot_max))                # distinct values across 2000 resamples
mean(boot_max == max(trial$sbp_0))      # how often the resample max is THE max
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
The resampled maximum can never exceed the observed maximum, and it equals it
when a unique largest observed value is drawn at all — probability
1 − (1 − 1/*n*)^*n*^ ≈ 0.63.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
The bootstrap distribution of a maximum is a spike at the observed value with a
short left tail. It can be a poor approximation to sampling a new maximum from the population. **Increasing B cannot fix that mismatch.**
:::


## Two packages you should know exist {.smaller}

Not installed here — this is a pointer, not a demonstration.

```r
# boot: the classical implementation. Statistic takes (data, indices).
library(boot)
b <- boot(trial, statistic = function(data, i) med_diff(data[i, ]), R = 10000)
boot.ci(b, type = c("perc", "basic", "bca"))

# rsample: tidymodels. Resamples as a tibble of splits.
library(rsample)
bootstraps(trial, times = 1000)
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
`boot.ci()` gives you **BCa** intervals — bias-corrected and accelerated — which
adjust interval endpoints using bias correction and an acceleration term. They still require a suitable resampling scheme and regularity conditions; they do not repair dependence or an unrepresentative sample.
:::


# 4 · Permutation tests {.section-divider}

## The null and the reassignment rule {.smaller}

In a completely randomized trial with fixed arm sizes, a randomization test of
the **sharp null of no effect for any participant** holds outcomes fixed and
reassigns treatment according to the actual randomization scheme.

For independent observational samples, unrestricted label permutation instead
needs exchangeability under the null, such as identical group distributions.

Equal means alone do not guarantee exchangeability when variances differ.
Blocked or paired randomization requires restricted reassignment.

## Shuffle the labels {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: perm-run
obs_mean <- mean_diff(trial)

set.seed(19)
P <- 999
perm_stat <- replicate(P, {
  shuffled <- sample(trial$arm)                 # permutation, not a bootstrap
  mean(trial$sbp_12[shuffled == "Treatment"]) -
    mean(trial$sbp_12[shuffled == "Placebo"])
})

c(observed = obs_mean, perm_mean = mean(perm_stat), perm_sd = sd(perm_stat))
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
Note what is **not** shuffled: `sbp_12` never moves. Only its label does. Jointly reordering outcome-label rows changes nothing. Breaking their pairing creates the reference distribution; the reassignment rule must match the design.
:::


## The null distribution {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: fig-perm
#| fig-cap: "Permutation null distribution of the mean difference, with the observed value."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| echo: false
ggplot(data.frame(stat = perm_stat), aes(stat)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey78", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs_mean, colour = "#8a4b1f", linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = obs_mean, y = Inf, label = "  observed", hjust = 0,
           vjust = 1.6, size = 4.5, colour = "#8a4b1f") +
  labs(x = "Mean difference in SBP at 12 weeks (mmHg)", y = "Permutations")
```

::: {.smaller}
Centred at zero **by construction**. The *p*-value is the proportion of this
histogram at least as extreme as the line.
:::


## Exact, or Monte Carlo? {.smaller}

With 4 patients per arm there are only `choose(8, 4)` = **70** possible label
assignments. You can enumerate **all** of them:

```{r}
#| label: exact-perm
small <- trial[c(1:4, 31:34), c("id", "arm", "sbp_12")]
obs_small <- mean_diff(small)

combos <- combn(8, 4)                    # every way to choose 4 "Treatment"
exact <- apply(combos, 2, function(k) mean(small$sbp_12[k]) -
                                      mean(small$sbp_12[-k]))

ncol(combos)                             # the entire reference set
round(mean(abs(exact) >= abs(obs_small)), 4)    # exact two-sided p-value
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
With 30 per arm there are `choose(60, 30)` ≈ 1.2 × 10^17^. So you
sample from them instead — that is all "Monte Carlo permutation" means.
:::


## A permutation *p*-value is never zero {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: perm-p
n_extreme <- sum(abs(perm_stat) >= abs(obs_mean))
n_extreme                                        # out of 999
```

. . .

```{r}
#| label: perm-p2
c(wrong = n_extreme / P,
  right = (n_extreme + 1) / (P + 1))
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
The observed arrangement **is** one of the possible arrangements. Counting it in
both numerator and denominator is not a fudge to avoid zero — it is the correct
count.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
With P = 999 and no sampled statistic as extreme, report the adjusted Monte Carlo p-value 0.001 and its limited resolution. Increase P if finer resolution is needed; do not report p = 0.
:::


## Interpret a permutation result {.smaller}

- A p-value measures incompatibility with the specified null and reassignment scheme.
- It does not by itself quantify the effect or remove confounding.
- Report the observed mean difference alongside the test result.
- This class computes tests; confidence intervals by inverting suitable tests
  are a further method, not an impossibility.

For an observational comparison, do not interpret a significant label-permutation
result as evidence of a causal treatment effect.

## Monte Carlo p-value uncertainty {.smaller}

```{r}
extreme <- sum(abs(perm_stat) >= abs(obs_mean))
c(adjusted_p = (extreme + 1) / (P + 1),
  min_reportable = 1 / (P + 1))
binom.test(extreme, P)$conf.int
```

The interval describes the tail probability estimated by independent random
permutations conditional on the observed data. It is not a confidence interval
for the treatment effect. Exact enumeration has no Monte Carlo sampling error.

## Practice: which reassignment is allowed? {.smaller}

Treatment was randomized separately within each site. A student permutes all
treatment labels across the pooled dataset.

What design feature has been lost? What must remain fixed?

## Practice: preserve the assignment mechanism {.smaller}

```r
shuffled <- trial$arm
for (i in split(seq_len(nrow(trial)), trial$site)) {
  shuffled[i] <- trial$arm[i][sample.int(length(i))]
}
```

Within-site assignment counts stay fixed. Use this rule only when it represents
the actual randomization; an arbitrary blocking variable does not establish validity.

# 5 · Choosing the resampling unit {.section-divider}

## The same cohort, three visits each {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: long-head
head(trial_long, 7)
c(rows = nrow(trial_long), patients = length(unique(trial_long$id)))
```

## Define the statistic for repeated visits {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: long-obs
diff_long <- function(data) {
  mean(data$sbp[data$arm == "Treatment"]) - mean(data$sbp[data$arm == "Placebo"])
}
obs_long <- diff_long(trial_long)
obs_long
```

::: {.smaller}
180 rows. **60 patients.** Hold on to that distinction — the rest of this block is
about which number is the sample size.
:::


## The naive row bootstrap {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: boot-rows
set.seed(21)
boot_row <- replicate(B, {
  idx <- sample(nrow(trial_long), replace = TRUE)   # 180 rows, independently
  diff_long(trial_long[idx, ])
})

c(estimate = obs_long, se = sd(boot_row))
round(quantile(boot_row, c(0.025, 0.975)), 2)
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
Perfectly reasonable code. Runs without complaint. Produces a clean, symmetric
histogram. The interval comfortably excludes zero.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
It is wrong, and nothing on this slide tells you so.
:::


## The cluster bootstrap {.smaller}

Resample **patients**, and take all of each patient's rows with them.

```{r}
#| label: boot-cluster
ids <- unique(trial_long$id)
rows_by_id <- split(seq_len(nrow(trial_long)), trial_long$id)   # id -> row numbers

set.seed(22)
boot_clu <- replicate(B, {
  picked <- sample(ids, replace = TRUE)              # 60 patients, with repeats
  diff_long(trial_long[unlist(rows_by_id[picked]), ])
})

c(row_se = sd(boot_row), cluster_se = sd(boot_clu),
  ratio = sd(boot_clu) / sd(boot_row))
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
Compare the two estimated SEs. With strong within-person dependence, independent row resampling understates uncertainty in this example.
:::


## Side by side {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: fig-unit
#| fig-cap: "Bootstrap distributions of the same estimate under two resampling schemes."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| echo: false
cmp <- rbind(
  data.frame(stat = boot_row, scheme = "Naive: resample rows (wrong)"),
  data.frame(stat = boot_clu, scheme = "Cluster: resample patients (right)")
)
cmp$scheme <- factor(cmp$scheme, levels = unique(cmp$scheme))
ggplot(cmp, aes(stat, fill = scheme)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 45, colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~scheme) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey72", gold)) +
  labs(x = "Difference in mean SBP (mmHg)", y = "Resamples") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.smaller}
Same data, same estimate, same statistic function. Only the **unit** changed.
:::


## Dependence limits information {.smaller}

The teaching generator uses a participant intercept with SD 12 and visit noise
with SD 4. Within each arm, its known correlation is:

```{r}
rho <- 12^2 / (12^2 + 4^2)
c(rho = rho, design_effect = 1 + (3 - 1) * rho,
  approximate_se_inflation = sqrt(1 + 2 * rho))
```

For equally sized clusters with this correlation structure, the design effect
explains why three correlated visits are not three independent participants.
This calculation uses the generator's parameters, not a fitted ICC estimate.

## Permuting at the wrong level, too {.smaller}

The same mistake, in the other half of the session:

```{r}
#| label: perm-unit
arm_by_id <- trial_long$arm[match(ids, trial_long$id)]

set.seed(32)
p_rows <- replicate(999, {
  s <- sample(trial_long$arm)                    # shuffles visits, not patients
  mean(trial_long$sbp[s == "Treatment"]) - mean(trial_long$sbp[s == "Placebo"])
})
```

## Permute patient assignments, then carry them to visits {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: perm-patient-unit
p_pats <- replicate(999, {
  assigned <- sample(arm_by_id)
  s <- assigned[match(trial_long$id, ids)]      # join by ID, not row order
  mean(trial_long$sbp[s == "Treatment"]) - mean(trial_long$sbp[s == "Placebo"])
})

c(p_row_unit = (sum(abs(p_rows) >= abs(obs_long)) + 1) / 1000,
  p_patient_unit = (sum(abs(p_pats) >= abs(obs_long)) + 1) / 1000)
```

::: {.smaller}
Compare the results and their resolution. **Randomisation happened to patients**, so the
permutation must too.
:::


## The resampling unit {.smaller}

| Design | Bootstrap or validation unit | Permutation restriction |
|---|---|---|
| Independent participants | Participant | Allowed participant assignments |
| Repeated visits | Participant with all visits | Keep one treatment per participant |
| Cluster randomized | Clinic or other randomized cluster | Reassign at cluster level |
| Matched pairs | Pair | Swap labels within pairs when justified |
| Time series | Dependence-preserving blocks or temporal splits | Requires a justified dependence model |

Sampling, randomization, and prediction targets can imply different rules.
State the rule before using `sample()`.


# 6 · Cross-validation {.section-divider}

## Prediction requires held-out outcomes {.smaller}

The target is error for new participants from a stated population, using
predictors available when the prediction will be made.

Training error evaluates data already used to fit the model. Cross-validation
instead repeats fitting on training folds and predicting an assessment fold.

We will predict 12-week SBP from baseline variables. A week-12 derived variable
would be unavailable at baseline, even if it greatly improved the reported score.

## The model interface for this exercise {.smaller}

```{r}
cv_data <- trial[, c("id", "arm", "age", "sbp_0", "sbp_12")]
fit_demo <- lm(sbp_12 ~ sbp_0 + age + arm, data = cv_data)
head(predict(fit_demo, newdata = cv_data), 3)
```

`lm(response ~ predictors, data = ...)` fits a linear regression.
`predict(fit, newdata = ...)` applies its learned coefficients.
These predictions are in-sample; Session 16 examines model objects in detail.

## Assign and inspect folds {.smaller}

```{r}
set.seed(1550)
fold <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(cv_data)))
table(fold, cv_data$arm)
stopifnot(length(fold) == nrow(cv_data), all(fold %in% 1:5))
```

Every participant belongs to one assessment fold and appears in training for
the other four fits. Balanced counts do not alone establish representative folds.

## One training and assessment split {.smaller}

```{r}
k <- 1
train <- cv_data[fold != k, ]
assess <- cv_data[fold == k, ]
stopifnot(length(intersect(train$id, assess$id)) == 0L)
fit <- lm(sbp_12 ~ sbp_0 + age + arm, data = train)
head(data.frame(id = assess$id, observed = assess$sbp_12,
                prediction = predict(fit, newdata = assess)), 3)
```

The assessment outcomes are used for scoring, not fitting.

## A complete set of held-out predictions {.smaller}

```{r}
prediction <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(cv_data))
seen <- integer(nrow(cv_data))
for (k in sort(unique(fold))) {
  test <- fold == k
  fit <- lm(sbp_12 ~ sbp_0 + age + arm, data = cv_data[!test, ])
  prediction[test] <- predict(fit, newdata = cv_data[test, ])
  seen[test] <- seen[test] + 1L
}
stopifnot(all(seen == 1L), all(is.finite(prediction)))
```

Preallocate with `NA`, not zero, so an unfilled prediction is detectable.

## Score each participant once {.smaller}

```{r}
loss <- (cv_data$sbp_12 - prediction)^2
c(cv_rmse = sqrt(mean(loss)),
  training_rmse = sqrt(mean(residuals(fit_demo)^2)))
tapply(loss, fold, mean)
```

RMSE has the outcome's units. Aggregate participant losses before taking the
square root. An unweighted average of fold RMSEs is generally a different quantity.

## Missing predictors require a learned rule {.smaller}

```{r}
cv_missing <- cv_data
cv_missing$sbp_0[c(2, 8, 17, 32, 46, 55)] <- NA_real_
train <- cv_missing[fold != 1, ]
assess <- cv_missing[fold == 1, ]
replacement <- mean(train$sbp_0, na.rm = TRUE)
train$sbp_0[is.na(train$sbp_0)] <- replacement
assess$sbp_0[is.na(assess$sbp_0)] <- replacement
```

Learn the replacement from training rows; apply the same value to assessment rows.
Mean imputation is a teaching example, not a general recommendation for missing data.

## Preprocessing belongs inside the loop {.smaller}

```{r}
cv_predict <- function(data, fold) {
  pred <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(data))
  for (k in sort(unique(fold))) {
    test <- fold == k
    train <- data[!test, ]; assess <- data[test, ]
    m <- mean(train$sbp_0, na.rm = TRUE)
    if (!is.finite(m)) stop("training baseline entirely missing")
    train$sbp_0[is.na(train$sbp_0)] <- m
    assess$sbp_0[is.na(assess$sbp_0)] <- m
    fit <- lm(sbp_12 ~ sbp_0 + age + arm, data = train)
    pred[test] <- predict(fit, newdata = assess)
  }
  pred
}
```

The same principle applies to scaling, feature selection, and tuning.

## Verify the prediction contract {.smaller}

```{r}
held_out <- cv_predict(cv_missing, fold)
stopifnot(length(held_out) == nrow(cv_missing),
          all(is.finite(held_out)))
sqrt(mean((cv_missing$sbp_12 - held_out)^2))
```

Also inspect training group sizes and factor levels. A predictor level never
seen during training needs a declared handling strategy, not a silent recode.

## A deliberately leaky version {.smaller}

```{r}
leaky_data <- cv_missing
global_mean <- mean(leaky_data$sbp_0, na.rm = TRUE)
leaky_data$sbp_0[is.na(leaky_data$sbp_0)] <- global_mean
leaky_prediction <- cv_predict(leaky_data, fold)
c(valid = sqrt(mean((cv_missing$sbp_12 - held_out)^2)),
  leaky = sqrt(mean((cv_missing$sbp_12 - leaky_prediction)^2)))
```

The assessment covariates influenced the imputation rule. The scores may be
close, and leakage need not improve every realization. Validity follows the
information flow, not which score happens to be smaller.

## Diagnose leakage before comparing scores {.smaller}

| Step | Valid location |
|---|---|
| Fixed, prespecified unit conversion | Can be applied to all rows |
| Mean imputation or scaling estimated from data | Training fold |
| Choose features using outcome associations | Training fold, with selection validated |
| Select a model or tuning parameter | Inner validation, separate from final evaluation |
| Compute RMSE | Held-out outcomes after predictions are fixed |

A fixed rule is different from a rule estimated using assessment data.

# 7 · Validation design {.section-divider}

## Compare with a simple benchmark {.smaller}

```{r}
baseline_prediction <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(cv_data))
for (k in sort(unique(fold))) {
  baseline_prediction[fold == k] <- mean(cv_data$sbp_12[fold != k])
}
c(training_mean_benchmark =
    sqrt(mean((cv_data$sbp_12 - baseline_prediction)^2)),
  regression = sqrt(mean((cv_data$sbp_12 - prediction)^2)))
```

Use the same folds for each candidate. More predictors need not improve prediction.

## Stratified folds {.smaller}

```{r}
make_folds <- function(arm, k = 5) {
  fold <- integer(length(arm))
  for (i in split(seq_along(arm), arm)) {
    fold[i] <- sample(rep(seq_len(k), length.out = length(i)))
  }
  fold
}
```

## Inspect the stratified fold composition {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: stratified-fold-table
set.seed(1551)
table(make_folds(cv_data$arm), cv_data$arm)
```

Stratification can stabilize composition. It does not repair dependence or
make a rare category large enough for every fold.

## Repeated cross-validation {.smaller}

```{r}
cv_rmse_once <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  f <- make_folds(cv_missing$arm)
  p <- cv_predict(cv_missing, f)
  sqrt(mean((cv_missing$sbp_12 - p)^2))
}
scores <- vapply(1561:1570, cv_rmse_once, numeric(1))
summary(scores)
```

Repeated splits describe sensitivity to fold assignment on this dataset.
They are not independent new studies; do not treat their SD as a sampling SE
or their range as a population confidence interval.

## Grouped and temporal validation {.smaller}

| Deployment question | Appropriate split idea |
|---|---|
| Predict a new participant | Keep all visits of a participant together |
| Predict at a new clinic | Hold out clinics |
| Predict future outcomes | Train on earlier observations; assess later observations |

```r
ids <- unique(trial_long$id)
id_fold <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = length(ids)))
row_fold <- id_fold[match(trial_long$id, ids)]
```

Random row folds answer the wrong question if the same participant appears on both sides.

## Selection and final evaluation {.smaller}

Trying many models and reporting the lowest CV error uses the evaluation data
to make a selection. The selected score can be optimistic.

Use a prespecified candidate, an untouched test set, or nested cross-validation:

1. An outer split reserves data for evaluation.
2. Inner training splits choose features and tuning parameters.
3. Refit the selected procedure on outer training data; predict outer assessment data.

After evaluation, a final model can be fitted to the intended full training set.

## Lab route and exit check {.smaller}

1. Bootstrap a treatment-minus-control mean difference within arms.
2. Compare Monte Carlo and exact permutation calculations.
3. Build checked folds and held-out predictions with fold-specific imputation.
4. Compare valid and leaky preprocessing, then repeat the fold assignment.
5. State how the procedure changes for repeated visits or a new clinic.

**Explain:** Which uncertainty shrinks with more bootstrap draws?
What makes a prediction held out?

- [R bootstrap confidence intervals](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/boot/html/boot.ci.html)
- [rsample V-fold cross-validation](https://rsample.tidymodels.org/reference/vfold_cv.html)
- [rsample grouped V-fold cross-validation](https://rsample.tidymodels.org/reference/group_vfold_cv.html)

## Summary {.smaller}

- Bootstrap, permutation, and cross-validation answer different questions.
- The resampling unit must preserve the design's dependence structure.
- Permutation validity rests on exchangeability under the null.
- Preprocessing learned outside a training fold leaks information.
- Finite resampling adds Monte Carlo variability that should be recorded.
